claims.text: Grain-boundary-mediated plasticity governs creep resistance in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
An ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high density of high-angle grain boundaries impedes dislocation motion during sustained high-temperature stress.
An ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high density of high-angle grain boundaries impedes grain-boundary sliding during sustained high-temperature stress.
Severe plastic deformation combined with intermediate-temperature annealing will refine the coating's grain structure.
Severe plastic deformation combined with intermediate-temperature annealing will increase the density of high-angle grain boundaries.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment produces an ultrafine-grained microstructure containing a dense network of high-angle grain boundaries.
Refined grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Refined grain boundaries inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
Inhibiting dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding distributes plastic deformation and delays rapid creep.
Relative to a coarse-grained baseline, the ultrafine-grained coating will have a lower creep rate.
Relative to a coarse-grained baseline, the ultrafine-grained coating will have a higher strain to failure.
Electron microscopy will show reduced grain-boundary sliding in refined regions of the ultrafine-grained coating.
Electron microscopy will show reduced dislocation motion in refined regions of the ultrafine-grained coating.
The predicted improvement applies at temperatures of approximately 0.5–0.6 Tm and sustained loads of approximately 0.7 times the yield stress.
At significantly higher temperatures or stresses, grain growth may diminish the benefits of grain-boundary engineering.
Long-term exposure to high temperatures may cause ultrafine grains to coarsen.
Thermally induced grain coarsening may reduce the effectiveness of high-angle grain boundaries in impeding creep.
